You can also put the tips of your fingers on the table and "walk" them forward and backwards, left to right, or write the alphabet. (I had to do that after my accident.) You put more force on them as you're able to, and this will help restore/keep dexterity. When I was in my bike accident, I smashed up both hands pretty badly but wouldn't let them operate - which meant a lot of PT. I'm healthy so it only took about 6 months and it was just my hands and one wrist, the rest of me was fine.

If you struggle with putting weight on your hands in a controlled fashion, you can actually just get the wrist weights (for doing the finger walking exercise) or just rest a book on the back of your hand while you do it. Your basic goal would be to walk your hands just like you're playing scales on a piano.

If you're diligent about this, you'll start to notice improvement within 6 weeks, probably sooner. It should tire your finger muscles out - not make them hurt more than you can stand. If it's truly painful, see a medical professional.

Never, ever play until your fingers hurt like hell. Never. Do NOT do that. You can screw up the nerves irrevocably. If your fingers start to hurt, do not play. I'm not kidding. Take a break, try again - that includes hurting from the pressure of pressing the stings. Build those callouses up slowly, they will come. You can, and may very well, cause permanent injury. You'll lose dexterity and sensitivity, on top of that you can start to lose feeling in different parts of your hands or all the way up to your forearms. Stop if it's painful.

That bullshit about playing until your fingers bled? Yeah, don't do that. That's not a terribly bright idea. (We're all guilty of it, but we're not supposed to do that.)

Now, what you'd be doing is setting the flow of current though the amp when the amp is idle. This is a fine balance between the flow of current at idle and at peak. You surely don't want to push more amps into it than you're rated for - and you also don't want to put too few. You're aiming for the best of both worlds - which is a compromise between the two.

On top of that, there's the life of the tube. If you're pushing too many electrons through the system, you will age the components faster - in this case, namely the tubes. If you put too many through the system, it lets out a blue puff of smoke and you swear a lot. On a really bad day, you hear a thump and a buzz. That's a really bad day. On the shittiest day of your life, it'll make that big thump and buzz noise and then it lets out the magic smoke. That's not a good day. That day has just become horrible.

I don't know how to do your model. I'm mostly a Marshall man. On a really, really horrible day - it'll do all that while you didn't change anything - at all. Some places have dirty, dirty power. You'll be up on stage and you'll hear the thump and get the familiar whiff of ozone that tells you the magic smoke escaped. This is why you always, always carry spares.
